name: Fatima Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Fatima, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenhill, which is a community-owned farm on the edge of town, about 60 hectares. We've got 90 ewes, 400 laying hens, a few pigs, and two big polytunnels of vegetables for our box scheme, which goes to about 300 households every week. My mornings are the hens and the sheep, afternoons are picking and packing boxes. I love lambing, even the cold nights, and I hate the packing shed on a Thursday when everything's late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do things stand outside work, at home and with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a flat above the bakery on Mill Street with my partner Yusuf, who drives the number 12 bus. Between us we just about cover rent and bills, and there's usually less than a month's money in the account. The farm pays the going rate, which isn't much, and it lives on a council grant that gets renewed every three years. I do use AI a bit, I get a chatbot to tidy up the weekly box newsletter, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the hype was always about making rich people richer. If AI just tidies up newsletters and spreadsheets, I'm fine with that. Farming was always going to be about soil and weather, not apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worries in that picture are the same ones I've got today. The council grant comes up for renewal next spring, and if it's cut, Greenhill drops to two paid staff and I'm the newest. AI doesn't change any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, hens, sheep, boxes. I'd keep using the chatbot for the newsletter, and maybe ask it to help with the grant report, because that's always a nightmare. And I'd try to get Yusuf and me to put his overtime money into savings instead of the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit relieved, but the grant thing still sits there. It's like a dentist appointment you can't cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the grant were cut next spring, what would you do that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the members' meeting and fight for it, because 300 families rely on those boxes. If the council cuts the Greenhill grant, I'm the newest of three paid workers, so I can count to what happens next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI might help with the grant report. Have you tried that yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, last year. It wrote something that sounded like a bank, so I rewrote half of it. Still, it got me past the blank page, which is the worst bit.

say: AI hype was mostly about **making rich people richer**.
Farming stays about **soil and weather**, not apps.
She is **fine with AI** tidying up newsletters and spreadsheets.
think: Her real risk is the **council grant** renewal next spring, not AI.
If the grant shrinks, she's the **newest worker** and likely to go.
do: Keep running the **hens, sheep and boxes** at Greenhill.
Use the chatbot for the **grant report** as well as the newsletter.
Move Yusuf's **overtime money** into savings instead of weekends out.
feel: **Relieved** about AI, but the **grant worry** stays.
S0.quote: If the council cuts the Greenhill grant, I'm the newest of three paid workers, so I can count to what happens next.
fieldNote: She frames even the calm picture around a **funding cliff** she already faces.
She's a **practical** AI user who rewrites what the tool gives her.
Her loyalty is to the **300 households** on the box scheme as much as to the job.

steps.text: Keep running the hens, sheep and box scheme at Greenhill
Use the chatbot to draft the council grant report
Save Yusuf's overtime pay instead of spending it at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should do the boring bits so people have more time for the real work. But I'd also say watch who gets the savings, because it's never the workers. I'd put that on the Greenhill members' page, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every Monday I spend half a day on box orders, swaps and customer emails, and that's exactly what AI would take. So my hours could drop from five days to four and a half, which is real money for us. The polytunnels and the sheep are safe for years, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to set up the AI ordering system myself, so I'm the one who knows how it works. I'd ask the members' meeting to promise that any time saved goes into growing more food, not into cutting hours. And I'd look at the short course in organic certification at the college, because that's paperwork a machine won't sign off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. I feel like I've got a say at Greenhill, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Yusuf, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buses don't drive themselves yet, so he'd be okay for a while. He'd be more worried about the app that plans the routes, because it already makes his shifts worse. He says the app doesn't know where the schools are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd set up the system yourself. Isn't that a bit like building your own replacement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but someone will build it, and I'd rather it's someone who loves the farm. At a community farm, the person who sets up the computer gets to decide what the saved time is for.

say: AI should do **the boring bits** so people have more real work time.
Workers should watch **who gets the savings** from AI.
think: AI would take her **Monday admin**, the box orders, swaps and emails.
Her days could drop to **four and a half**, though the hands-on work is safe.
do: Volunteer to set up the **AI ordering system** herself.
Ask the members' meeting to put saved time into **growing more food**.
Look at the college course in **organic certification**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but steadied by having **a say** at Greenhill.
S1.quote: At a community farm, the person who sets up the computer gets to decide what the saved time is for.
fieldNote: She sees **owning the change** as safer than resisting it.
Her progressive view shows in asking **who gets the savings**.
The household's second risk is **Yusuf's bus job**, though it's not urgent here.

steps.text: Set up the AI box-ordering system at Greenhill herself
Ask the members' meeting to protect paid hours
Enrol in the college's organic certification short course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public plan, now, like after a war. Housing, income, retraining, all of it. I'd be on every march about it and I'd say so online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work gets the three extra years, but Yusuf's job doesn't. Self-driving buses are partly thinking machines, so his route could be gone by 2029, and then it's my wage alone on rent we can barely cover with two. That's the bit that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Yusuf the first week and cut everything we can, the second phone, the streaming, the car if he loses the bus. I'd push the Greenhill members to turn the farm into a food hub for people losing work, because that keeps us useful and funded. And I'd be at the bus drivers' union rallies with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and also angry. It's a lot to carry in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're fine, because she worries. Then I'd ask if her spare room is still free. I'd tell my mum we're fine, and in the same breath ask whether her spare room is still empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap for robots change anything you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a window. In those three years I'd try to make myself the person who runs things at Greenhill, the planting plan, the volunteers, not just the hands. Robots might pick lettuce, but someone has to decide what we grow and who it's for.

say: The country needs a **public plan** for housing, income and retraining.
She'd be on **every march** and say so online.
think: Her hands-on work gets **three extra years**, but Yusuf's bus job doesn't.
Rent on **one wage** would barely be covered.
do: Cut the **second phone**, streaming and maybe the car in the first week.
Push Greenhill members to become a **food hub** for people losing work.
Join Yusuf at the **bus drivers' union** rallies.
feel: **Frightened** and **angry** at how fast it comes.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum we're fine, and in the same breath ask whether her spare room is still empty.
fieldNote: Her biggest risk is a **household earner**, not her own job.
She uses the robot gap to move toward **planning and organising** at the farm.
The **spare room** line shows how near the edge they live.

steps.text: Cancel the second phone and streaming with Yusuf
Propose turning Greenhill into a food hub for people losing work
Ask her mum about moving into the spare room
March and campaign for a public plan on income and housing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to plan, so I'd say there's no excuse this time. I'd want the council and the government to publish what happens to farm and transport workers. I'd write to our MP, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, Yusuf could retrain before the buses go, maybe as a technician at the depot. And I'd have time to move into running Greenhill rather than just working it. It's still a squeeze, but it doesn't feel like falling off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the organic certification course this year, and a volunteer coordinator course next year. I'd push Yusuf to ask the bus company about depot training before everyone else does. And I'd start saving properly, 100 a month into a separate account Yusuf can't see on his app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels like worry you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said an account Yusuf can't see. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's lovely, but if money's visible, it gets spent on a takeaway after a late shift. I'd tell him it's there, I just wouldn't put it on the shared app. It's an old trick my aunt taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Greenhill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who's 58 and only does the heavy lifting and the tractor. He hates screens and he's got nobody. At Greenhill (the community farm she works on) I'd worry most about Pete (her workmate), who's 58, hates screens, and has only ever known how to lift things.

say: Five years leaves **no excuse** for not planning.
She'd **write to her MP** for the first time.
Government should publish what happens to **farm and transport** workers.
think: Yusuf could **retrain at the depot** before the buses go.
She could move into **running Greenhill**, not just working it.
do: Take the **organic certification** course this year and coordinator training next year.
Push Yusuf to ask about **depot training** early.
Save **100 a month** into a separate account.
feel: **Worried**, but with things she **can act on**.
S3.quote: At Greenhill (the community farm she works on) I'd worry most about Pete (her workmate), who's 58, hates screens, and has only ever known how to lift things.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **two-person plan** for the household.
She shows care for **Pete**, an older colleague who'd be left behind.
The hidden **savings account** is a small, practical habit from family.

steps.text: Complete the organic certification course this year
Save 100 a month in a separate account
Write to her MP about farm and transport workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift, so I'd say let's use it. Retrain people, change how land is owned, make sure community farms get the machines too. I'd say that at the members' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'd be 40, and the robots could do my hands-on work. But by then I want to be the one running a farm like Greenhill, not picking for it. And Yusuf and I would have to decide about kids with all this in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the certification and the coordinator course, slowly, one a year. I'd ask Greenhill's board about a path to farm manager in five years. And Yusuf and I would talk properly about whether to have a child in the next few years or wait to see how work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly, with a little cloud over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The question about children. How does AI change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not AI exactly, it's money and whether we'll both have work. With thinking machines arriving in 2036, Yusuf (her partner) and I keep asking whether a baby fits before or after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Greenhill look like in 2039, in your best version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice the size, robots doing the weeding, and people like me running it with the members. More families on the box scheme, cheaper food. I'd be proud of that.

say: Ten years is **a gift** to retrain people and rethink land ownership.
Community farms should **get the machines** too.
think: By 40 she wants to be **running a farm**, not picking for it.
Work worries shape the **decision about children** with Yusuf.
do: Take one course a year, **certification** then **coordinator** training.
Ask Greenhill's board about a path to **farm manager** in five years.
Talk with Yusuf about **having a child** soon or waiting.
S4.quote: With thinking machines arriving in 2036, Yusuf (her partner) and I keep asking whether a baby fits before or after.
fieldNote: With time, her plan shifts from survival to **career growth** at Greenhill.
The baby question shows AI reaching into **family plans**, not only jobs.
She pictures robots **doing the weeding** under community control.

steps.text: Take one farm management course a year
Ask Greenhill's board about becoming farm manager in five years
Decide with Yusuf when to try for a baby

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of Yusuf. My hands-on work buys me time, but his bus job and our rent don't wait. What would help is a proper public plan: help with rent, paid retraining, and money for community farms so we can take on people who lose work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the food. If machines make food cheaper, great, but only if the people growing it can still afford to buy it. I grow vegetables for 300 families, and some weeks Yusuf (her partner) and I can't afford the box we pack.

headlineQuote: I grow vegetables for 300 families, and some weeks Yusuf (her partner) and I can't afford the box we pack.
portrait: Fatima is 27 and works with **sheep, hens and vegetables** at Greenhill, a community-owned farm.
She rents a flat with **Yusuf, a bus driver**, on two low wages and almost no savings.
She's progressive and practical, using AI **now and then** and wanting workers to share the gains.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** mainly because of **Yusuf's job**, then eases with more time.
With time, she aims to **run Greenhill** rather than just work there.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Yusuf's bus job could go fast and the **rent** depends on both wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** with rent help and **paid retraining**.
Funding for **community farms** to take on people who lose work.
